title: Dodgers May Bench Ohtani in Game 3 Amid MLB Trade Rumors Surge
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts is reportedly weighing a drastic move for the franchise’s marquee player: benching Shohei Ohtani for Game 3 of the World Series. The decision comes after the Japanese phenom struggled through a sub‑par performance in Game 2, showing clear signs of fatigue that have left the Dodgers’ bid for a historic three‑peat hanging by a thread.

Ohtani, who entered the series as a dual‑threat ace and designated hitter, appeared noticeably off‑balance in Milwaukee’s 7‑4 victory. He recorded just one hit in five at‑bats and his fastball velocity dipped by several miles per hour, prompting medical staff to note that he was “well below 100 percent physically.” While the Dodgers have a deep roster, Ohtani’s unique blend of power and pitching makes him a linchpin in any lineup. Removing him, even temporarily, would be a bold statement about the team’s willingness to prioritize long‑term health over short‑term heroics.

The Dodgers entered the series as heavy favorites, having clinched three consecutive National League pennants and a World Series title just two years ago. Yet the Brewers, buoyed by home‑field advantage and a resilient bullpen, have forced the series to a decisive third game. In Game 2, Milwaukee’s bullpen, anchored by veteran reliever Trevor Megill, stifled the Dodgers’ offense, while the Brewers’ offense capitalized on timely hitting to secure the win. The loss has exposed a lingering vulnerability in Los Angeles: an overreliance on Ohtani’s production. When he is contained, the Dodgers’ depth players have struggled to generate consistent run support, a trend that could become a liability if the series extends further.

Analysts are divided on the potential benching. Some argue that keeping Ohtani in the lineup, even at reduced effectiveness, could still provide a psychological boost and force the Brewers to adjust their pitching strategy. Others contend that a short rest could preserve his arm and restore his explosiveness for a potential Game 4, should the series go that far. The Dodgers’ medical team reportedly monitors Ohtani’s shoulder and lower back closely, noting lingering soreness that could worsen with another high‑intensity outing. In past postseason scenarios, teams have opted to sit star players to protect them for the remainder of the series—a tactic famously employed by the 2016 Chicago Cubs when they rested key pitchers before a decisive Game 7.

If Roberts decides to sit Ohtani, the responsibility will shift to the likes of Tyler Glasnow, who could start the next game, and to the bench batters who must step up offensively. The Dodgers’ bench depth, featuring players such as Kiké Hernández and Mookie Betts, offers a viable, though not ideal, alternative. However, the psychological impact of benching a player of Ohtani’s stature could ripple through the clubhouse, testing the team’s cohesion at a critical juncture.

Looking ahead, the Dodgers must balance the immediate desire to stay alive in the series with the broader goal of preserving their star for a potential championship run. Should Ohtani return refreshed, his dual‑role could once again tilt the series in Los Angeles’ favor. Conversely, a prolonged absence could force the Dodgers to rely on a more conventional, pitcher‑first approach, testing the depth of their roster and the strategic acumen of their coaching staff. As Game 3 looms, all eyes will be on Roberts’ decision, a choice that could shape not only the outcome of this World Series but also the future health and legacy of one of baseball’s most electrifying talents.
